preamble.summary: The plague of darkness revisited — Egypt trapped in supernatural darkness while Israel walks in light. A meditation on the psychology of terror and the self-imprisonment of the wicked.
preamble.remarkable: The most vivid psychological horror writing in biblical literature. The darkness is not merely physical but spiritual — the Egyptians are paralyzed by their own guilty conscience, haunted by sounds and visions. This chapter influenced medieval theology of hell as self-chosen darkness.
preamble.friction: The Latin tenebrae carries both physical and spiritual connotations that English 'darkness' only partially captures. Jerome's vocabulary for psychological states (formido, timor, stupor) requires careful differentiation.
preamble.connections: Exodus 10:21-23 (ninth plague), John 3:19 (loved darkness rather than light), 1 John 1:5 (God is light). The fire-that-gives-no-light motif connects to medieval depictions of hell.

verses.text_latin: Magna enim sunt iudicia tua Domine et inenarrabilia verba tua propter hoc indisciplinatae animae erraverunt
verses.rendering: For great are your judgments, Lord, and your words beyond telling; therefore undisciplined souls went astray.
translator_notes: Inenarrabilia (unspeakable, beyond narration) sets the tone — what follows defies ordinary description.

key_terms.note: Stronger than 'indescribable' — implies narrative itself fails before God's judgments

verses.text_latin: Dum enim persuasum habent iniqui posse dominari nationi sanctae vinculis tenebrarum et longae noctis compediti
verses.rendering: For while the wicked supposed they could lord it over the holy nation, they themselves lay bound in fetters of darkness and prisoners of a long night,
translator_notes: Vinculis tenebrarum (fetters of darkness) — the darkness itself becomes chains. A reversal: those who enslaved others are themselves enslaved.

key_terms.note: Influenced Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 imagery of angels bound in darkness

verses.text_latin: clausi sub tectis fugitivi perpetuae providentiae iacuerunt
verses.rendering: shut in under their roofs, fugitives from eternal providence, they lay helpless.

verses.text_latin: Nec enim quae continebat illos spelunca sine timore custodiebat quoniam sonitus descendens perturbabat illos et personae tristes illis apparentes pavorem illis praestabant
verses.rendering: For not even the cave that held them kept them without fear, since disturbing sounds descended upon them and grim phantoms with gloomy faces appeared to them.
translator_notes: Personae tristes (sad/grim masks or faces) — the Latin persona originally meant a theatrical mask, adding an uncanny quality to these apparitions.

verses.text_latin: Et ignis quidem nulla vis poterat illis lumen praebere nec siderum limpidae flammae inluminare poterant illam noctem horrendam
verses.rendering: No force of fire could give them light, nor could the bright flames of the stars illuminate that dreadful night.

verses.text_latin: Apparebat autem illis subitaneus ignis timore plenus et timore perculsi illius quae non videbatur faciei aestimabant deteriora esse quae videbantur
verses.rendering: There appeared to them only a sudden fire, full of terror; and struck with fear at that sight which could not be seen, they thought what they saw was worse still.
translator_notes: A paradox: they fear what they cannot see more than what they can — the psychology of darkness.

verses.text_latin: Et magicae artis adpositi erant risus et sapientiae gloriae correptio cum contumelia
verses.rendering: The delusions of their magic arts were put to shame, and their boasted wisdom was rebuked with disgrace.

key_terms.note: Egyptian sorcery powerless against divine darkness — connects to Exodus 7-8 magicians

verses.text_latin: Illi enim qui promittebant timores et perturbationes expellere se ab anima languente ipsi pleni timore ridiculo languebant
verses.rendering: For those who promised to drive fears and terrors from a sick soul were themselves sick with ridiculous fear.

verses.text_latin: Et si nihil illos ex monstris perturbabat transitu animalium et serpentium sibilatione commoti peribant trementes
verses.rendering: Even if nothing among the terrors disturbed them, yet scared by the passing of animals and hissing of serpents, they perished trembling,

verses.text_latin: et aerem quem nulla vi quis effugere posset negantes se videre
verses.rendering: refusing to look even at the air, which no one can escape.

verses.text_latin: Cum sit enim timida nequitia dat testimonium condemnationis semper enim praesumit saeva perturbata conscientia
verses.rendering: For wickedness is by nature cowardly and gives testimony to its own condemnation; a troubled conscience always assumes the worst.
translator_notes: One of the most psychologically acute verses in Scripture — wickedness is self-condemning through its own fear.

key_terms.note: This phrase shaped Western moral psychology — the guilty conscience torments itself without external accuser

verses.text_latin: Nihil enim est timor nisi proditio cogitationis auxiliorum
verses.rendering: For fear is nothing but the surrender of the aids that reason offers.
translator_notes: A philosophical definition of fear as reason's abdication — influenced Aquinas and scholastic moral psychology.

key_terms.note: Fear defined as betrayal by one's own thinking — remarkably modern psychological insight

verses.text_latin: Et dum ab intus minor est expectatio maiorem computat inscientiam eius causae de qua tormentum praestat
verses.rendering: And while from within the expectation is less, it counts the ignorance greater than the cause which brings the torment.

verses.text_latin: Illi autem qui inpotentis vere noctis eosdemque ab infimis et ab altissimis inferis supervenientis eandem somnum dormientes
verses.rendering: But they, sleeping the same sleep during that truly powerless night which came upon them from the depths of inescapable Hades,

verses.text_latin: aliquando monstrorum exagitabantur timore aliquando animae deficiebant traductione subitaneus enim illis et insperatus timor supervenerat
verses.rendering: were sometimes driven by monstrous phantoms, and sometimes paralyzed in their souls by treachery; for sudden and unexpected fear overwhelmed them.

verses.text_latin: Deinde si quisquam ex illis decidisset custodiebatur in carcere sine ferro reclusus
verses.rendering: Then if any of them fell down, he was kept shut up in a prison not made of iron,

verses.text_latin: Si enim rusticus quis erat aut pastor aut agri laborum operarius praeoccupatus esset ineffugibilem sustinebat necessitatem
verses.rendering: for whether one was a farmer or a shepherd or a laborer working in the field, he was seized and endured an inescapable fate,

verses.text_latin: Una enim catena tenebrarum omnes erant conligati sive spiritus sibilans aut inter spissos arborum ramos avium sonus suavis
verses.rendering: for all were bound by one chain of darkness — whether it was a whistling wind, or a sweet bird-song among the thick branches of trees,
translator_notes: Una catena tenebrarum (one chain of darkness) — all bound alike regardless of status. The ordinary sounds of nature become sources of terror.

key_terms.note: Connects to Jude's 'chains of darkness' and 2 Peter's 'pits of darkness'

verses.text_latin: aut vis aquae decurrentis nimium aut sonus validus praecipitatarum petrarum
verses.rendering: or the rushing force of running water, or the loud crash of falling rocks,

verses.text_latin: aut ludentium animalium cursus invisus aut mugientium valida bestiarum vox aut resonans de altissimis montibus echo
verses.rendering: or the unseen course of bounding animals, or the roaring voice of savage beasts, or an echo rebounding from the highest mountains —

verses.text_latin: haec illos deficere faciebant prae timore
verses.rendering: all these things paralyzed them with terror.
translator_notes: The cumulative list — ordinary nature sounds become instruments of divine judgment when conscience is guilty.
